title: Security fixes: four decisions before we build

steps.path: Pictures inside the assistant's messages, in every kind of chat
steps.headline: Should pictures from websites in the assistant's replies wait for a tap before they load?
steps.today: When a reply includes a picture from a website, the app loads it straight away. This happens in every chat, Claude Code chats included.
steps.problem: A tricked assistant can hide private information inside a picture's web address. The moment the reply appears, that information is sent to whoever owns the website. There is no tool and no question.
steps.proposal: A picture from a website shows as a small box naming the site, with a Show button. One tap loads it. Pictures from your own files still show normally.

options.label: Tap to show
pros: Closes this leak in every chat, including Claude Code chats.
Replies rarely include web pictures, so you will seldom see the box.
cons: A web picture you actually want costs one tap.

options.label: Never load them
pros: Simplest; there is nothing to tap.
cons: A web picture you want can never be seen inside the chat.

options.label: Leave as today
cons: The best-known way AI apps leak data stays open.

steps.path: The approval cards that appear inside a chat
steps.headline: After the assistant reads a private settings file, should its first visit to each new website ask you?
steps.today: Reading any file and visiting any website never ask. That was your 5 September decision: questions are for actions that change things.
steps.problem: A web page can tell the assistant to read a file holding saved passwords, then visit a website with that file's contents in the address. Both steps happen silently.
steps.proposal: Keep reads and web visits free, with two additions. First, a short list of pure password files the assistant can never open. Second, only in a chat that has read a hidden settings file in your home folder, one question the first time it contacts each new website.

options.label: Both additions
pros: Chats that never touch those files see nothing new.
It blocks the step that actually carries data out.
cons: A chat that read something like your shell settings asks once per new website, usually zero to three times.
A chat left running on its own can pause on that question.

options.label: Password list only
cons: Misses mixed files that hold passwords alongside ordinary settings.
Any file left off the list is a gap an attacker can use.

options.label: Ask for every site
options.summary: Ask the first time any chat contacts a new website, the way Claude Code does.
cons: Questions return in ordinary research chats, undoing most of the 5 September change.

steps.path: The installer on Windows and Mac, and the Update button in the app
steps.headline: Should we pay about $219 a year so installs show your company name instead of warnings?
steps.today: Windows shows 'Unknown publisher' when installing YouCoded. On a Mac, people must open System Settings, press Open Anyway and type their password.
steps.problem: Students and everyday users give up at those warnings, and anyone technical reads them as a sign the project is not serious.
steps.proposal: Windows signing through Microsoft ($9.99 a month) and Apple's developer program ($99 a year). You would need a website and email address on a domain the company owns, a free business ID number and a photo-ID check. Approval takes days to weeks. The free part happens either way: the app checking that each update is genuine, and the broken Update button working again.

options.label: Windows and Mac
pros: Installs show Destin's Adventures, LLC as the publisher right away.
Mac installs become a normal double-click.
cons: A few hours of paperwork, then waiting on approvals.
The Windows warning fades over weeks as downloads build trust, not instantly.

options.label: Windows only
pros: About $120 a year, and only Microsoft's paperwork.
cons: Mac users keep the Open Anyway steps.

options.label: Neither for now
cons: The warnings stay on every install.

steps.path: The review pages you answer before work is merged
steps.headline: Can these seven fixes skip the full new-feature process and reach you as one before-and-after review?
steps.today: New features go through a questions page, a fresh-eyes tester, reviewers, a written definition of done and a final acceptance round.
steps.problem: These are fixes with a clear direction, and most change nothing you can see. The full process adds days without adding much.
steps.proposal: Every fix still gets automated tests and a fresh code reviewer. Everything you can see comes to you on one before-and-after page before anything merges: the password field, the wait message, the picture box, the website question and the update error.

options.label: Light route
pros: You still see and approve every visible change.
cons: No separate fresh-eyes tester reads the new wording first.

options.label: Full for visible ones
options.summary: The full process for the password and website-question changes; the light route for the rest.
pros: The two changes people will see most get the most scrutiny.
cons: Those two fixes arrive several days later.
